Question: I'm joining the school band. Should I play oboe, baritone horn, or French horn? (I'm advanced at piano).
Answer: This is a really tough question to answer. I once worked with a private music academy that had a retention rate more than 4 times that of any other schools or academies. The difference was this: All students had to spend time on every main classification of instrument (strings, brass, woodwinds, percussion) for their first year of study. There's no real way to know what pair of shoes fits you the best until you put them on and go for a long stroll. After I finished undergrad as a French horn major, I became an orchestra director for a few years. I had very little experience with strings, but they were desperate for a teacher, and I was willing to take the job. The first time I tried playing a cello was during my first week on the job. The first scale I played made me a little sick to my stomach. The instrument just felt like a part of my body right away. I could feel a connection come easily that I've always had to work a little to get on the horn. The sound made sense to me. I should've tried cello when I was a kid, but my school didn't have an orchestra - just band. There's no way to know what would have happened if I had chosen to play cello, but I can't say with certainty that horn was a perfect fit for me. As a teacher, I'm aware of certain aspects of my physical makeup that work against me. It makes me wonder. What I do know is that if I had spent some time playing cello, I would have fallen in love with it, and I would have probably transferred to a school with an orchestra. So try them all. Even the ones you don't think you'll like. Decide the top 3 things that you like about each instrument and then see if you enjoy trying to make one or more of those things happen. Any instrument will have challenges. It will be your love of the things you appreciate the most that will bring you the most joy. That love will let you practice a little better. Make you want to pull more beauty out of a note. Make your heart swell and put a lump in your throat. Good luck!

Question: Is a blowing horn a brass instrument or a woodwind instrument?
Answer: If the sound is produced by the lip or lips vibrating, then it is considered a brass instrument. If a reed does the vibrating, it's a woodwind. Classification of instruments is usually based on how the sound is generated. For instance, a harp is a string instrument because the sound is produced by plucking. Even though a piano produces a similar sound, and also has strings like a harp, it is classified as a percussion instrument because the sound is produced by a hammer striking the strings.

Question: What was the most entrepreneurial thing you ever did as a child?
Answer: I got in a lot of trouble that first week of kindergarten, and it all came to a head with my first business venture. I really didn't understand the purpose of school. I understood what they said it was all about, but it seemed extremely chaotic. Other children seemed vicious and unpredictable. On my second day of school in the morning while we were putting our coats away, I showed the kid next to me what I made the night before. Just a simple paper popper. I had an arts and crafts book at home that showed you how to make them. My classmate was impressed. He said his older brother knew how to make them, but he wouldn't show him how or even let him have one. I just gave him the one I had. That evening, I had what I thought was a great idea. A foolproof way to make friends. I made 5 poppers. I even decorated them with pictures of lightening bolts and tiger claws. I also reinforced the seams with tape so they'd be stronger. I honestly had no intention of selling them. I planned on choosing five kids that I wanted to be friends with, and then just giving them away. Instead, I made the mistake of showing them to the boy from the day before. He immediately asked for one - I said no - He offered me 5 cents - I said yes. I sold the rest before the morning bell rang 5 minutes later. I finally understood what school was for! My mom had laughed at me when I'd asked her how much I'd be paid for working at school. Now who's laughing? The next day, I showed up with 10 poppers. The problem was - somebody had taken apart one of my poppers and figured out how to make their own. I didn't sell even one. Plus, one of the girls in my class was making these: Fortune tellers! I was competing with open source developers and the mysterious universe. That's a lot to deal with when you're only 5. That evening, I got out the craft book and learned how to make these: I made 20. I figured that I should decorate them somehow. And that's where things went horribly wrong. A boy on my bus that day had a neat shape written on the back of his hand. I had asked him what it was. He said "my dad said it means really bad war." This fit my ninja stars perfectly. I was pretty sure that the design of the stars themselves was too complicated to be easily copied - at least it would let me regain the market and give me time to check out another origami book at the library. The swastikas would send a message to the fortune teller girl. I'd seen a lot of shows on TV. I knew I was supposed to send a message. I put swastikas on both sides. I sold 6 of those stars before Mrs. McVay delared martial law in our classroom. I don't know how she found out. Maybe she had her own paper fortune teller. She went through everybody's things and confiscated ALL origami. She also told us all that the swastika was a horrible symbol of hate that an evil man once used while he had millions of people murdered. She said he murdered children and their parents. You know, Mrs. McVay never personally outed me during that whole thing. She retired 2 years later, and passed away before I graduated high school, so I never got to talk to her as an adult. I imagine she saw a little kid being swept up in dreams of grandeur. I gave everybody their money back at lunch on my own. Several years ago, when my niece was 5, I started to show her how to fold a popper. She just laughed, took the paper from me, and showed me how to fold a swan. I still can't make a swan that looks right. I hate origami.

Question: Why do hornists lift their horns, like in some parts of "The Rite of Spring"?
Answer: That technique is referred to amongst horn players as "bells up". Different composers have different ways of asking for this, but they all want basically the same thing. They're looking for a less veiled, much more strident tone. A sound that hearkens back to our roots. A hunting horn sound. Less like this: Stravinsky's Firebird, Finale Horn Solo:  More like this: Chasse à courrèe.wmv:  The modern horn evolved from what was basically a signaling device. Not only does playing bells up look pretty cool, it allows the sound to project a little better. When done correctly, the player should be using a much more open right hand position inside the bell and putting as much edge on the sound as the conductor will let them get away with.

Question: Can one suffocate on a CPAP machine?
Answer: No. If for some reason your mask became completely blocked, your mouth will fall open and you'll be just fine, if you're using a nasal mask. Some people are naturally "mouth breathers" and need to use a CPAP mask that covers the entire nose and mouth in order to maintain airway pressurization. Even in this case, if the machine stopped working, there's still plenty of air that can pass through the unit to keep you alive. Think of a window fan blowing air into a room. Even if the fan is turned off, air is still free to pass through the fan. This is essentially how a CPAP machine works. Now, let's say through some weird circumstances that the hose to your mask became completely clogged, and you were using a full face mask. You'll still be fine. You'll basically have what polysomnographers call a "full arousal". At first, you'll struggle a bit to breathe, just like you do during sleep apnea. Once your blood oxygen levels dip low enough, your subconscious brain will arouse your consciousness to deal with the problem. You'll most likely wake up for just a few seconds to yank the mask off and then go right back to sleep. So quit worrying and use your CPAP like you know you're supposed to. It's not going to kill you, but not using it eventually will. :-)

Question: What's more interesting: play a particular song or play an instrument?

Answer: I started to write my own interpretation of the lyrics, then I thought I'd check Wikipedia. The chili peppers have always been very straightforward about explaining their lyrics, and the Wiki about "Give it Away" is excellent. Taken from http://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Give_It_Away_(Red_Hot_Chili_Peppers_song) The lyrical meaning behind "Give It Away" is centered on the philosophy of selflessness and altruistic behavior.[4] The song is titled after its most prevalent lyrical phrase "give it away", which is taken from an experience Kiedis had with his former girlfriend—punk rock singer Nina Hagen—in the early 1980s.[4]Hagen was several years Kiedis' senior and became a role-model during his drug addiction to heroin: "she realized how young and inexperienced I was then, so she was always passing on gems to me, not in a preachy way, just by seizing on opportunities."[7] When Kiedis was looking through her closet he came across a jacket he liked, and commented to Hagen that it was "really cool".[7] Upon expressing this, Hagen immediately told him to keep it. Her reasoning behind this selflessness was due to an attempt to constantly make her life more enjoyable, and explained to Kiedis that "if you have a closet full of clothes and you try to keep them all, your life will get very small. But if you have a full closet and someone sees something they like, if you give it to them, the world is a better place."[7] The act was something that affected Kiedis significantly because he had never before experienced such an enlightening ideology on life. Growing up in Los Angeles he had always thought differently from Hagen; instead of giving material possessions away and being free thinking the vocalist believed one must take what they want as no one will provide for you.[7] Instead, he now adopted Hagen's philosophy: "It was such an epiphany that someone would want to give me her favorite thing. That stuck with me forever. Every time I'd be thinking 'I have to keep,' I'd remember 'No, you gotta give away instead.' When I started going regularly to [drug and alcohol] meetings, one of the principles I had learned was that the way to maintain your own sobriety is to give it to another suffering alcoholic. Every time you empty your vessel of that energy, fresh new energy comes flooding in."[7] Flea's bassline for the song allowed Kiedis to recall this incident and he believed the music paired perfectly with the lyrics.[4] During the verses, Kiedis departs from the idea of unselfishness and sings about a variety of topics including long-time friend River Phoenix, musician Bob Marleyand various sexual themes including fertilityand lust.[8]

Question: As a beginner on the French horn, what is the best way to achieve mastery?

My old teacher William Slocum (he played in NY Phil as well as the Cleveland Orchestra under Szell) had many great words of wisdom. I remember one afternoon I gave a recital and just totally crashed and burned. It was terrible. He approached me backstage. I felt like crying. Being a great horn player actually comes last in the process. First you have love music so much that you're driven to put in the time and effort necessary to get good at the horn. If it were as simple as following some sort of system, then everyone would play the horn and it would be nothing special.

Question: Is this Atkinson H300 double French horn any good?
Answer: It looks like it's in pretty good shape. The leadpipe appears to be in excellent condition, and the rest of the horn looks like it's in good shape as well. No apparent damage in the usual areas. The big question is the valves. There's no way to see them in a photo. Rotary valves should have a very close tolerance in order to create the kind of compression that is necessary to play well. If a horn is cared for properly, valves can last many decades. If someone doesn't oil their valves regularly, eats sugary foods and drinks, and doesn't snake out their leadpipe once a week, they can ruin a set of valves in just a few years. This means that the horn could look great on the outside, but be a wreck on the inside. That said, the outside condition usually reflects the inside condition when it comes to student horns. The seller seems to have a good reputation. I would say that it's worth the risk at that price to get it, try it out (or have a professional or your teacher play it), and then pay to ship it back if you don't like it.

Question: How do I train for a 5k run, if I'm used to running longer distances and have never been in a race?
Answer: Start doing a HIIT (high intensity interval training) routine 2 or 3 days a week. It's really simple. I use a 8/12 second cycle. Basically, I do an easy jog for 5 minutes. Then 20 minutes of 8 seconds of all out sprint alternating with 12 seconds slow trot (60 cycles). Then I end with a 5 minute cool down trot followed by stretching. The stretching is vital to prevent injury. The HIIT routine will boost your VO2 max allowing your muscles to perform longer and stronger. On the other days you run, have a metronome with you. You can download one for free on a smartphone or buy a tiny one cheap from most music stores. Figure out what your general foot cadence is. Get the metronome beat to match your steps. Once you figure out your current pace, start bumping it up 3-5 beats per minute each time you run. This will speed up your pace like you won't believe. Good luck!

Question: I just learned that my mom has been having a one year long affair. How do I tell her I know, and should I even tell my dad?
Answer: This is a very touchy situation. For a long time, I felt that the thing to do would be to let the cheater know what you observed and then give them a little time to come clean on their own. If they wouldn't come clean, then I would tell the person who was being cheated on myself. I still feel that way. I wish I could tell you exactly how to go about this and what to say, but I can't. The one most important piece of advice that I can give you is to not let any anger show in your words or body language when you talk to your mom. You actually have to be the adult in this situation. Ask her to give you one or two minutes to say what you need to say, and then tell her if she wants to respond to you right away, fine. Or if she needs a day or two before she's ready to talk to you, that's fine too. Just let her know that you love both of your parents equally, but that you just don't know what to do. It's really important that you emphasize that you aren't coming to her out of anger, but out of serious concern for both she and your dad. Also, decide on boundaries for yourself before you talk to her. Make it very clear to her that you wish you'd never seen/heard/learned what you did, but you can't undo it or just forget. Keep in mind that this sort of thing happens all the time all over the world to all sorts of people. It's nothing unusual. It sucks for sure, but you can get through this if you keep a clear head and only act out of love and compassion. If you hold yourself to that concept, it'll keep you sane if things start to seem a little bit crazy. Anger will blind you. Compassion will open your eyes. Question: How does it feel when your best friend with whom you shared everything dies? What all do you go through after his death?
Answer: Several years ago, my best friend from childhood died. Brad was a pharmacist driving to work one morning and pulled out in front of a semi truck. It happened at an intersection that we both knew well. We rode our bikes there as kids. We raced our cars there as teenagers. When we were in elementary school, we were inseparable. We had this thing we would do where we would have conversations with each other, but we'd only say the first couple of words and then the other would finish the thought. It would really creep people out. I've never had another friendship like that. Brad's mom committed suicide when we were in the 5th grade right before school let out for the summer. After it happened, the school psychologist told Brad's father that he and his brother needed to be kept isolated from other kids to allow them to grieve. I wasn't allowed to go over to his house. This continued for the whole summer. When we started school in the fall, he wouldn't speak to me. He would even join in with some of the school bullies occasionally and make fun of me. At the time, I was completely confused. I thought the death of his mom must've messed up his mind. We became unfriendly strangers. Toward the end of our senior year, we got paired up by a teacher to do a final project for a class that we were both taking. I went over to his house one evening to work on it, and within a minute we were both laughing our asses off. Hours later when I was on my way out, we were standing in the hallway outside of the room where his mom died. I said "Do you still miss her". "Of course, why would you care"? No one had ever told Brad about the school psychologist's instructions. He thought that I had abandoned him, and that I blamed him for his mom's suicide. The regrets hanging there in the air were massive. We finished school a few days later and then both became busy with our summer jobs and preparing to leave for college. We fell out of touch. We never spoke again after that evening at his house. When I heard of his death, I didn't really feel anything for a few days. Then one morning I was sitting in my car and watched as two boys rode past me laughing like idiots. Then the memories came flooding in and the tears came flooding out. Every few years when I make it back to my hometown, I always drive around the old neighborhood and reminisce. I once watched an interview with actor Sally Fields where she was asked how she portrays sadness so well on screen. She explained that every tragedy and loss in her life leaves a wound on the inside. She said that when she needs to show grief, she reaches inside and opens that wound up a little. This explanation really resonated with me. I don't think about Brad very often, but that inner wound is still there.

Question: What are some of the funniest stories from your childhood where you learned an important lesson from your dad?
Answer: I used to hate getting up early on Sundays for church. My Dad would always say "We're leaving in fifteen minutes. However you're dressed, that's how you're going." Me and my brothers would always laugh because we thought he was joking. One Sunday when I was 5, I decided to test him. 10 minutes before we were supposed to leave, I was in my underpants only. 5 minutes before - underpants and one sock. Time to go - underpants and socks only. Dad laughed and said "Alright, get in the car." I still thought he was bluffing. I figured he had my church clothes in the car hidden somewhere. The closer we got, the more I started thinking I'd made a mistake. When we were a block away from the church I said "I can't go inside like this!" Dad said "of course not, you'll have to stay in the car. Here's a book." He then proceeded to park right in front of the church entrance where everyone would walk past. The book he left me was a manual on car repair. He did leave me the emergency blanket from the trunk and cracked the windows a little (it was early fall). Embarrassed doesn't even come close to how I felt. Everyone that walked past saw me and asked what was going on through the window. I bet dad got a lot of high gives that day (he was the church organist). I think that was the first time it really sunk in that my dad was/is a man of his word. In hindsight, I bet he was hanging out in the lobby checking on me every few minutes. I've never told him how much that day caused me to respect him. I should probably do that really soon.

Question: What are some of the funniest lies that parents have told their children?
Answer: My Dad always told me and my brothers about the magic class that he took in college. The two tricks we never figured out until we were adults and he finally told us... 1. When we would pull into the garage at night he would show us an intricate series of hand gestures that would magically make the interior dome light turn on. We would try to mimic his magic hand movements, but it never worked. He was just opening his door slightly. 2. He would have us choose any book off of the shelf, hand it to him, and then lay it flat on a table. He'd then take a nickel out of his pocket, close his fist around it and punch the book. He'd hold up his fist, open his hand, and there'd be no coin. Then he'd have one of us shake the book and the nickel would fall out. The trick - He had two nickels. He'd palm the first one before we handed him the book and then slip it between the pages as he set it down. Then he'd grab the other nickel and show it to us. Question: What are the potential long term effects of over-wearing contact lenses - specifically vis oxygen exposure to the eye?
Answer: I have a good friend that is an optometrist. Here's how he explained it to me... Your cornea is naturally gas permeable. Think of a screen, like on a screen door. Throughout the day, there's all sorts of microscopic debris that sticks to the "screen". Tears wash away or dissolve much of the debris, and it gets washed into your tear ducts (like gutters). The debris that can't be removed by tears is dealt with by small blood vessels just under the surface of the cornea. Modern contact lenses are also gas permeable, so when they're clean, no worries. When you leave them in two things happen. First, they get clogged with not just debris in the air - proteins in tears also stick to them. Second, the dirtier they get, the more your body starts to see them as a foreign body. This causes the blood vessels under the cornea to start growing up through the cornea in preparation to attempt to absorb the contact lenses into the body and then have the internal immune system deal with them. This process generally takes a long time because the irritation isn't severe (unless you get a bad eye infection - that'll speed up the process). By the way, once those blood vessels grow through the cornea, they don't grow back. And once they get thick enough, it starts to effect the quality of your vision. My optometrist always checks carefully under my upper eyelids to see how much blood vessel growth is going on. This area will show the worst of what's going on because it's the part of the eye that receives the least oxygen due to being covered by the eyelids most of the time. So take your lenses out at night and keep them clean. Even if they're extended wear. It's worth the trouble.

Question: How can I improve my very poor freestyle swimming speed? I'm 30 years old and 5′10." I can barely make it across the 25m pool. My feet are a 8.5 US size and my ankles are not too flexible.
Answer: You just need to figure out how to move efficiently through the water. Swimming is flying. You have to learn to glide. When I walk onto a pool deck and I have to decide who to share a lane with - I count strokes and find someone near my own stroke count. Start off by swimming a normal 25 at 60 percent speed. Count how many strokes you take. Now push off the other side and experiment with seeing how few strokes you can possibly take to reach the other side. Don't worry about speed. When you reach, make yourself as long as possible from the tips of your fingers to the tips of your big toes. Use a nice gentle kick. Your kick is 60 percent of your thrust, but it sounds like your hydrodynamics aren't working right. You'll find that just as airplanes do, swimmers also have a stall speed (unless you're fat). On the flip side, if your body position and stroke are wacky, there will also be a certain speed you can't move beyond. This isn't something that you can learn from watching Phelps on YouTube. It's all about feel. Figure out your stroke count and then watch one of his races and count his. Then realize he's swimming in a 50yd pool. Then feel the hairs stand up on the back of your neck when you realize those Olympics folks are beyond amazing. Here's a good website that explains things a little better... http://totalimmersion.net/blog/whats-the-right-stroke-count/

Question: Is there an objective, perceivable, difference between the sound of a horn with screw-on bell and fixed bell?
Answer: The answer is yes, there is a difference between how the horn sounds and plays before the bell is cut and after. There's really no way to make a blanket statement about cut bell vs. fixed bell horns because there are simply too many variables to give a scientific answer that would hold water. Every horn is different. I have had many students have their bells cut over the years and what I've observed is this: horns with a thicker bell don't really sound different, they just feel a little bit different to the player. Neither good or bad, just different. Horns with a thinner bell show a bigger difference. The sound is clearer with more punch at the front end of the note. When it comes right down to it, cut bell vs. fixed bell isn't really about the sound. Could you tell the difference between someone running with slip on running shoes vs. laced shoes? It depends on the runner. It's about having options. With a cut bell you have unlimited options (well, whatever your wallet can handle).
